newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: U.S. diplomat named to run disputed Bosnian town.
newsitem.headline: U.S. diplomat named to run disputed Bosnian town.

text.p: The international community's High Representative for Bosnia, Carl Bildt, said on Friday he had appointed Bill Farrand, a senior U.S. diplomat, as supervisor of the hotly disputed Bosnian town of Brcko.

In a statement released in Vienna ahead of an international conference on the volatile town, claimed by both Serbs and the Moslem-Croat federation, Bildt said: "I warmly welcome Bill Farrand to the Office of the High Representative as my deputy and supervisor for Brcko."

"He is a vastly experienced foreign service officer and brings all of the right qualities to this very important job," he added. Farrand is a career State Department diplomat with on-the-ground experience in Eastern Europe.
Bildt's announcement came ahead of a high-level meeting on the town's future, attended by all key parties in the Bosnian peace process, at Vienna's historic Hofburg palace.
U.S arbiter Robert Owen three weeks ago ruled that the Sava river port town would be put under international supervision pending a final decision next year on its status.
Farrand's job will be to strengthen democratic institutions and oversee implementation of the Dayton peace accord that ended Bosnia's 43-month war but was almost scuppered by the Brcko issue.

Brcko was captured by Bosnian Serbs early in the 1992-95 war and purged of its mainly Moslem-Croat pre-war population. Serbs had threatened to resume war if they were denied control of Brcko, which sits on a narrow land corridor linking eastern and western Serb-controlled territories.
The Moslems and Croats in turn claim Serb control over Brcko would reward so-called ethnic cleansing and deprive them of access to the Sava and Danube rivers and other main European waterways.

Washington's envoy to the Balkans, John Kornblum, has said the arbiter's decision to avoid a clear resolution of the issue was "definitely enough" to prevent renewed fighting between Bosnian Serb and Moslem forces.
Bildt has said the ruling sought to strike a balance in "the mother of all difficulties in the Bosnian peace process".
Farrand will be empowered to set up a multi-ethnic police force and issue regulations to local police.
The supervisor should also ensure full freedom of movement, oversee the return of Moslem and Croat refugees and implement an economic revitalisation programme for the Brcko area.
